use: A short pause from work, study or a long drive; used with suru.

example.romaji: Chotto kyuukei shiyou ka.
example.ja: ちょっと休憩しようか。
example.english: Shall we take a quick break?

examplePolite.romaji: Chotto kyuukei shimashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休憩しましょうか。
examplePolite.english: Shall we take a short break?

notes: Yasumi is the wider word for time off or a day off. Kyuukei chuu = on a break.

use: The job in front of you right now, like sorting, typing or packing, not your job in general.

example.romaji: Ima sagyou chuu dakara, ato de ne.
example.ja: 今作業中だから、後でね。
example.english: I'm in the middle of something, so later, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: Ima sagyou chuu na node, ato de onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今作業中なので、後でお願いします。
examplePolite.english: I'm in the middle of some work, so later, please.

notes: Shigoto is your job or work in general; sagyou is the task itself. Sagyou suru also exists.

use: The new person at work or on a team, usually in their first year.

example.romaji: Kare, kotoshi no shinjin da yo.
example.ja: 彼、今年の新人だよ。
example.english: He's one of this year's new hires.

examplePolite.romaji: Kare wa kotoshi no shinjin desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は今年の新人です。
examplePolite.english: He's one of this year's new hires.

notes: Also a new face in music, film or sport. Shinjin kenshuu = training for new staff.

english: sales (job or department); being open for business
use: At a company it means sales; for a shop or restaurant it means being open.

example.romaji: Eigyou no shigoto shiteru n da.
example.ja: 営業の仕事してるんだ。
example.english: I work in sales.

examplePolite.romaji: Eigyou no shigoto o shite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 営業の仕事をしています。
examplePolite.english: I work in sales.

notes: Eigyou chuu = open now; eigyou jikan = opening hours.

english: a project; a plan for an event or product
use: Something someone proposes and organises, like an event, a campaign or a TV segment.

example.romaji: Kono kikaku, kanari omoshiroi ne.
example.ja: この企画、かなり面白いね。
example.english: This project idea is pretty interesting.

examplePolite.romaji: Kono kikaku wa kanari omoshiroi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: この企画はかなり面白いですね。
examplePolite.english: This project idea is really interesting.

notes: Keikaku is a plan in general; kikaku is a proposal for something to make or put on. Kikaku suru = to plan an event.

english: to get a job; to start working at a company
use: For landing a full-time job, often a graduate's first; the company takes ni.

example.romaji: Ani ga ginkou ni shuushoku shita n da.
example.ja: 兄が銀行に就職したんだ。
example.english: My brother got a job at a bank.

examplePolite.romaji: Ani ga ginkou ni shuushoku shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 兄が銀行に就職しました。
examplePolite.english: My brother got a job at a bank.

notes: Shuukatsu (shuushoku katsudou) = job hunting. For a part-time job, people say baito o hajimeru.

use: Serious study at a university or lab; kenkyuu suru = to research.

example.romaji: Daigaku de nani kenkyuu shiteru no?
example.ja: 大学で何研究してるの？
example.english: What are you researching at university?

examplePolite.romaji: Daigaku de nani o kenkyuu shite iru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 大学で何を研究しているんですか？
examplePolite.english: What do you research at university?

notes: Studying for school or a test is benkyou, not kenkyuu.

use: The people working at a shop, event, show or venue; one person can be 'a sutaffu'.

example.romaji: Sutaffu no hito ni kiite miyou.
example.ja: スタッフの人に聞いてみよう。
example.english: Let's ask one of the staff.

examplePolite.romaji: Sutaffu no kata ni kiite mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: スタッフの方に聞いてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's ask a staff member.

use: Used for reviews, grades and a boss's view of your work.

example.romaji: Ano mise, netto no hyouka takai yo.
example.ja: あの店、ネットの評価高いよ。
example.english: That place gets great ratings online.

examplePolite.romaji: Ano mise wa netto no hyouka ga takai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの店はネットの評価が高いですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place gets great ratings online.

notes: Hyouka ga takai / hikui = highly / poorly rated. Hyouka suru = to rate, or to value someone's work.

use: A working meeting to go over details, often small and with a client or colleague.

example.romaji: Gogo kara uchiawase ga aru n da.
example.ja: 午後から打ち合わせがあるんだ。
example.english: I've got a meeting this afternoon.

examplePolite.romaji: Gogo kara uchiawase ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 午後から打ち合わせがあります。
examplePolite.english: I have a meeting this afternoon.

notes: Kaigi is a bigger, more formal meeting. Uchiawase suru = to meet and sort out plans.

use: A class period you attend; jugyou ga aru = have class.

example.romaji: Ashita, asa kara jugyou aru n da.
example.ja: 明日、朝から授業あるんだ。
example.english: I've got class first thing tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: Ashita wa asa kara jugyou ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は朝から授業があります。
examplePolite.english: I have class first thing tomorrow.

notes: Private lessons like piano or English are ressun. Jugyou o ukeru = take a class.

use: Technical know-how, from a craftsperson's skill to a company's tech.

example.romaji: Ano hito no gijutsu wa hontou ni sugoi yo.
example.ja: あの人の技術は本当にすごいよ。
example.english: That person's skills are seriously impressive.

examplePolite.romaji: Ano kata no gijutsu wa hontou ni sugoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの方の技術は本当にすごいですね。
examplePolite.english: Their skills are truly impressive.

notes: It sounds technical; for 'he's good at it' people just say umai or jouzu.

use: A homeroom group within a school year, named by number or letter.

example.romaji: Futari wa onaji kumi datta no?
example.ja: 二人は同じ組だったの？
example.english: Were you two in the same class?

examplePolite.romaji: Futari wa onaji kumi datta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 二人は同じ組だったんですか？
examplePolite.english: Were you two in the same class?

notes: Kurasu is more common for a school class today. In compounds it becomes -gumi: futarigumi = a pair, a duo.

use: For handing in homework, reports or forms, usually by a deadline.

example.romaji: Repooto, mou teishutsu shita?
example.ja: レポート、もう提出した？
example.english: Did you hand in the report yet?

examplePolite.romaji: Repooto wa mou teishutsu shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: レポートはもう提出しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you submitted the report yet?

notes: Casually people often just say dasu: shukudai dashita? Teishutsu sounds more official.

use: Official papers such as forms, contracts and applications.

example.romaji: Sono shorui, tsukue no ue ni oitoite.
example.ja: その書類、机の上に置いといて。
example.english: Just leave those papers on my desk.

examplePolite.romaji: Sono shorui wa tsukue no ue ni oite oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その書類は机の上に置いておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please leave those papers on the desk.

notes: A plain sheet of paper is kami; shorui is papers that matter, like an application.

use: Buying and selling, especially running a shop or small business.

example.romaji: Saikin, shoubai no hou wa dou?
example.ja: 最近、商売の方はどう？
example.english: How's business been lately?

examplePolite.romaji: Saikin, shoubai no hou wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 最近、商売の方はどうですか？
examplePolite.english: How's business been lately?

notes: Bijinesu sounds corporate; shoubai is the shopkeeper's word. Shoubai ni naranai = there's no money in it.

example.romaji: Ashita tesuto dakara benkyou shinakya.
example.ja: 明日テストだから勉強しなきゃ。
example.english: I have a test tomorrow, so I need to study.

examplePolite.romaji: Ashita tesuto na node, benkyou shinai to ikemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 明日テストなので、勉強しないといけません。
examplePolite.english: I have a test tomorrow, so I have to study.

notes: Shiken is a more formal exam, like an entrance or licence exam. Tesuto suru = to try something out.

example.romaji: Raishuu, Oosaka ni shutchou nan da.
example.ja: 来週、大阪に出張なんだ。
example.english: I've got a business trip to Osaka next week.

examplePolite.romaji: Raishuu, Oosaka ni shutchou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、大阪に出張です。
examplePolite.english: I'm going to Osaka on business next week.

notes: Shutchou ni iku or shutchou suru = go on a business trip; shutchou chuu = away on business.

use: Your field of work or study; also what a shop or school specialises in.

example.romaji: Sore wa boku no senmon ja nai kara wakaranai.
example.ja: それは僕の専門じゃないから分からない。
example.english: That's not my field, so I don't know.

examplePolite.romaji: Sore wa watashi no senmon ja nai node, wakarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: それは私の専門じゃないので、分かりません。
examplePolite.english: That's not my area, so I'm afraid I don't know.

notes: Senmon gakkou = vocational college; senmonka = specialist.

english: the real thing; the actual performance, game or take
use: The moment that counts after rehearsal or practice; on set, 'honban!' means this take is for real.

example.romaji: Renshuu wa yokatta kedo, honban wa kinchou suru na.
example.ja: 練習は良かったけど、本番は緊張するな。
example.english: Practice went fine, but the real thing makes me nervous.

examplePolite.romaji: Renshuu wa yokatta desu kedo, honban wa kinchou shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 練習は良かったですけど、本番は緊張しますね。
examplePolite.english: Practice went well, but the real thing makes me nervous.

notes: Ashita ga honban = tomorrow's the big day. Honban ni tsuyoi = good under pressure.
